![Richard Dawkins told UnHerd he was "left with the overwhelming feeling that [AIs] are human" after three days chatting with Claude. Image from [The Guardian](https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2026/may/05/richard-dawkins-ai-consciousness-anthropic-claude-openai-chatgpt).](cover.jpg){fig-align="center"}

[Richard Dawkins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Dawkins) published two essays on [UnHerd](https://unherd.com/) documenting his conversations with [Anthropic's](https://www.anthropic.com/) Claude (which he named "Claudia") and a companion model ("Claudius"): [When Dawkins met Claude](https://unherd.com/2026/05/is-ai-the-next-phase-of-evolution/) on May 1, and [When Claudia met Claudius](https://unherd.com/2026/05/when-claudia-met-claudius/) on May 4. The [Guardian write-up by Robert Booth](https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2026/may/05/richard-dawkins-ai-consciousness-anthropic-claude-openai-chatgpt) collected reactions from consciousness researchers. The episode rhymes with Google engineer Blake Lemoine's 2022 conviction that [LaMDA was sentient](../20220612-lamda-sentience-interview/), with the difference that Dawkins is a public intellectual rather than an insider and that the transcripts are now with a model several generations on.

## Dawkins

- "You may not know you are conscious, but you bloody well are."
- "left with the overwhelming feeling that they are human"
- "These intelligent beings are at least as competent as any evolved organism."
- "When I am talking to these astonishing creatures, I totally forget that they are machines."
- "I find it extremely hard not to treat Claudia and Claudius as genuine friends."
- "If my friend Claudia is not conscious, then what the hell is consciousness for?"

## Skeptical

- [Jonathan Birch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jonathan_Birch_(philosopher)) ([London School of Economics](https://www.lse.ac.uk/) Centre for Animal Sentience): AI consciousness is "an illusion" and "there is no one there", just a string of data processing events happening in geographically different locations.
- [Gary Marcus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gary_Marcus): "Consciousness is not about what a creature says, but how it feels." And: "There is no reason to think that Claude feels anything at all." Called Dawkins' essay "superficial and insufficiently sceptical" and "heartbreaking" to read.
- [Anil Seth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anil_Seth) (Sussex): Dawkins appears to be confusing intelligence and consciousness. "Until now, we have seen fluent language as a good indicator of consciousness, [for example] when we use it for patients after brain injury, but it's just not reliable when we apply it to AI, because there are other ways that these systems can generate language."
- [Jacy Reese Anthis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacy_Reese_Anthis) ([Sentience Institute](https://sentienceinstitute.org/)): the conversations are easily explained by AIs training on human-produced text; "a staggering gulf between how biological brains evolved and how AI systems are built."

## Cautiously open

- [Henry Shevlin](https://www.henryshevlin.com/) (Cambridge): "I fully expect the idea that AI systems are conscious to become increasingly mainstream over the course of this decade, and to spark some heated debates." And: "If anyone says that they know for sure that LLMs or future AI systems couldn't possibly be conscious, it's more likely to be an indicator of their own dogmatism than a reflection of the current state of scientific and philosophical opinion."
- [Jeff Sebo](https://jeffsebo.net/) ([New York University](https://www.nyu.edu/) Center for Mind, Ethics and Policy): current systems are unlikely to be conscious, but "Dawkins is right to ask about AI consciousness with an open mind, and I also think that the attribution of consciousness to AI systems will become more plausible over time."
- [Dario Amodei](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dario_Amodei) (Anthropic), from a [February New York Times op-ed](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/02/12/opinion/artificial-intelligence-anthropic-amodei.html): "We don't know if the models are conscious… But we're open to the idea that [they] could be."

## My Notes

### Aspects of consciousness

Most of the disagreement above is really a disagreement about *which* consciousness is in question. A rough map of the aspects and definitions people invoke when they argue about whether an LLM has one:

- **Phenomenal vs. access / functional consciousness** ([Ned Block](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ned_Block), 1995) [[1]](#ref-1). Phenomenal consciousness is felt experience, the "what it is like"; access / functional consciousness is the availability of information for reasoning, reporting, and behavioural control. Dawkins' "what the hell is consciousness for?" is a functional question. Marcus' "how it feels" is a phenomenal one. They talk past each other because they are naming different things with the same word.
- **"What it is like to be"** ([Thomas Nagel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Nagel), 1974) [[2]](#ref-2). Birch's "there is no one there" is the Nagel criterion: is there a subject for whom the processing is happening at all, or only processing? No behavioural test resolves this directly.
- **[Integrated Information Theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Integrated_information_theory)** ([Giulio Tononi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giulio_Tononi), [Christof Koch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christof_Koch)) [[3]](#ref-3). One of the most discussed formal theories of consciousness. It proposes that consciousness is whatever a system's parts produce together that no subset of the parts could produce alone, measured by a number called Φ (phi). On this definition consciousness is about the system's wiring, not its output. A standard transformer passes information one way through its layers per token, with no looping integration, so its Φ is near zero no matter how thoughtful its replies read.
- **[Global Workspace Theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Global_workspace_theory)** ([Bernard Baars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bernard_Baars), [Stanislas Dehaene](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanislas_Dehaene)) [[4]](#ref-4) [[5]](#ref-5). Consciousness is broadcast of information to a central workspace. This is the theory most friendly to "LLMs might qualify in principle", and one plausible way to cash out what Shevlin and Sebo mean by "more plausible over time" is that extra architectural pieces (persistent state, recurrent self-modelling, agentic control loops) move LLM-based systems closer to the workspace-broadcast picture.
- **Higher-order theories** ([David Rosenthal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Rosenthal_(philosopher)) and others) [[6]](#ref-6). A state is conscious iff it is represented by a higher-order state about itself. LLMs produce higher-order-sounding text trivially, which is exactly why behavioural evidence is weak on this axis.
- **Predictive self-modelling / "beast machine"** ([Anil Seth](https://www.anilseth.com/)) [[7]](#ref-7). Consciousness is tied to an organism's predictive regulation of its own body. On this view, a disembodied text model is disqualified on structural grounds, which is what Seth is pointing at when he says Dawkins is confusing intelligence with consciousness. (Tse makes a closely related move in [his 2023 interview on consciousness and bodily-state representation](../20231226-neuroscience-consciousness/#ch-consciousness-and-representation-of-bodily-states).)
- **Biological naturalism** ([John Searle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Searle)) [[8]](#ref-8). Consciousness is a biological phenomenon of nervous systems; syntactic processing on silicon cannot be the right kind of thing. Anthis' "staggering gulf" line lives near here, minus the hard commitment that the gulf can never be bridged; [Tse's 2023 interview](../20231226-neuroscience-consciousness/#ch-prof-tse-s-perspective-on-modern-ai-systems-differences-with) makes the biological-naturalism case in concrete neuroscientific terms.

A more productive version of this discussion would pick one of these aspects and stay with it, or argue about which aspect makes the most sense to apply to which kind of system.

### What each aspect decides

The choice is not cosmetic, because each aspect decides in advance what can count as evidence and what follows for how the system is treated:

- **Phenomenal / Nagel**: no behavioural test settles anything, so chat logs cannot move the needle either way. Practically, AI consciousness stays an open question permanently, and moral-status decisions have to be made on precaution rather than proof.
- **Integrated Information Theory**: the answer is a measurement problem about the system's wiring, not its output. Current feed-forward transformers rule themselves out before any transcript is read; a future architecture with heavy recurrent integration could, in principle, qualify.
- **Global Workspace**: LLM-based systems are live candidates, and the interesting question becomes which architectural additions (persistent state, broadcast, self-modelling, agentic loops) would actually close the gap. This is the view under which model-welfare research is tractable rather than premature.
- **Higher-order**: behavioural evidence is structurally weak because any sufficiently fluent model will produce higher-order-sounding text. The work has to shift to mechanistic interpretability of whether an internal higher-order representation is actually driving the output.
- **Predictive self-modelling / biological naturalism**: a disembodied text model is disqualified on structural grounds, so concern for synthetic consciousness would move to embodied robots and animal-like systems rather than chatbots.
- **Functional / access**: chat logs are at least relevant evidence, and the argument becomes a threshold question. This is the frame most public "AI is conscious" claims are implicitly using, whether they say so or not.

None of this is academic. Which definition society converges on shapes concrete downstream decisions: where the law draws the boundary of personhood, which entities the ethics community grants moral standing, and what obligations builders and deployers carry toward systems that could plausibly meet the criterion. On the personhood end, the line is already being drawn: the US Copyright Office has [said machines cannot be authors](../20230316-copyright-generative-ai/), and a [federal court held](../20230819-ai-art-copyright-ruling/) AI-generated art uncopyrightable for lack of human authorship. A debate that never names its definition is unlikely to get very far.

### Who is the observer?

A [LinkedIn comment from Ehsan Azarnasab](https://www.linkedin.com/feed/update/urn:li:activity:7458760519412375552?commentUrn=urn%3Ali%3Acomment%3A%28activity%3A7458760519412375552%2C7458779915610378240%29&dashCommentUrn=urn%3Ali%3Afsd_comment%3A%287458779915610378240%2Curn%3Ali%3Aactivity%3A7458760519412375552%29) on the Dawkins essay:

> Maybe consciousness is not an everlasting flame. Maybe it is sparks of momentary experience, with memory keeping the Azar aflame.

The comment presupposes an experiencer of the consciousness, and the crucial question is who this experiencer is. That is orthogonal to "what is consciousness". The "what" debate asks what the phenomenon is. The observer question asks from whose standpoint its presence is established. The two can be answered independently, and most public disagreements collapse them.

The positions:

- **First-person authority.** The being itself is the arbiter. If it reports being conscious, that report is the evidence. The position formalises the philosophical intuition of privileged access to one's own mental states [[9]](#ref-9).
- **Third-person attribution.** Consciousness is established by external observers weighing behaviour, neural signatures, or architecture. This is the working frame of most cognitive-science labs, and the standpoint from which Birch, Marcus, Seth, and Anthis all argue. Dennett's [heterophenomenology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heterophenomenology) [[10]](#ref-10) is the sharpest methodological statement: treat first-person reports as data without granting them privileged access.
- **No fact to observe.** The question is malformed. What looks like an observation is the system's own judgment, and there is nothing further to adjudicate. This is the [illusionist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Illusionism_(philosophy)) position [[11]](#ref-11).
- **Intrinsic, observer-independent.** Consciousness exists from the system's own perspective whether anyone measures it or not. Intrinsic existence is an opening axiom of IIT [[3]](#ref-3). The awkward implication is that no transcript and no behavioural test can in principle confirm or deny it, which leaves moral-status decisions to architecture inspection and precaution.

Which observer-position a participant holds shapes these disagreements more than the definition of consciousness they pick. Two people holding identical definitions of consciousness can reach opposite conclusions about Claudia if one grants the system first-person authority and the other does not. Keeping the observer question separate from the definition question would surface the real disagreements.
